Nothing in PLAN.md/README accepts this: they call the JS kind "trusted local code" but describe command tools as "argv, no shell" with shell_exec disabled by default. One nit: the exact scenario token `"-c rm -rf ~/x"` as a single argv element would make bash fail with "invalid option", but a trivially different template/input (separate `-c` token, or program=sh with script placeholder) works, so the claim stands.

Reachable in principle, but it is the designed trust model, not a bypass: PLAN.md §137/§170 define custom tools as "trusted local" code at ask policy, and a js custom tool already has full host-process access at the same policy (node:vm with host objects passed in is explicitly not a boundary, custom.ts:5). shell_exec: never guards the model's unapproved direct shell; custom_tool_run always requires an approval card on create and on every run. The run card is not blind either: approvalPreview (loop.ts:120) prints the full inputJson, so the user sees `bash` and the argument verbatim, and the create card showed the {{input.program}} {{input.arg}} template (the finding's exact payload would also fail, since spawn with shell:false passes "-c rm -rf ~/x" as one token). Showing the resolved argv on the card would be a minor UX nicety requiring configDir to be threaded into approvalPreview, not a security fix.

refuted.claim: The client sends ping every 20 s but never checks that a pong comes back, so a half-open socket (laptop sleep, NAT timeout, proxy drop without FIN) is never detected: the UI stays 'online' and silently stops receiving frames.
reasons: Confirmed by reading the code paths. gui/web/src/ws/client.ts line 197 starts a 20 s setInterval that only calls send({t:'ping'}); nothing records when a frame or pong last arrived, and there is no timeout that closes the socket. The server does reply (gui/server/src/ws/hub.ts:151-152 sends {t:'pong'}), but the client reducer treats it as a pure no-op (gui/web/src/state/applyEvent.ts:152 `case 'pong': return { state, effects: NO_EFFECTS }`), so the reply is discarded. There is also no visibilitychange / navigator online-offline listener anywhere in web/src, so nothing else forces a reconnect after sleep. The server-side protection (hub.ts heartbeat: ws.ping() every 20 s and ws.terminate() after 60 s idle) does not help the client on a half-open connection: the terminate/RST never reaches a client whose NAT mapping or TCP path is gone, and until the OS retransmission timeout eventually fails a ping send (minutes), ws.readyState stays OPEN, so send() returns true, Composer/QuickActions/ApprovalCard/StatusBar all read connection==='online', and no onclose -> scheduleReconnect -> onHello -> run.subscribe{fromSeq} replay happens. The finding's "or ever" is slightly overstated (the client's own ping writes will eventually trip the TCP retransmit timeout and yield a close event), but the described window of a stale "Online" UI with silently dropped sends and no replay is real and unhandled. Severity low is appropriate.

The mechanism described (client pings, ignores pong) is accurate, but the consequence ("never detected", "stays Online forever") does not hold in practice, and the scenario is largely unreachable in the studio's default topology.

1. Default deployment is loopback. gui/server/src/config.ts:60 binds `127.0.0.1` unless CFD_HOST/CFD_ALLOW_REMOTE is set, and the web client connects to `window.location.host` (frames.ts:51). Over loopback there is no NAT, no proxy, and no half-open state: a laptop sleep pauses both ends together. On wake the server's own heartbeat (hub.ts:75-86, HEARTBEAT_MS=20 s, IDLE_CLOSE_MS=60 s) sees `lastActive` stale and calls `ws.terminate()`, which delivers a FIN/RST over loopback immediately, firing the client's `onclose` → `scheduleReconnect()` → hello → `run.subscribe{fromSeq}` replay and `reconcileRuns()`. So the exact "laptop sleeps mid-run" scenario self-heals within one server heartbeat tick.

2. Remote (opt-in) case is still bounded, not "never". The client is not passive: it *sends* a ping every 20 s. After sleep the server has already terminated the socket (60 s idle), so the client's next ping segment is answered by a TCP RST from the server host → browser fires `onclose` within ~20 s. Only if the NAT/proxy silently black-holes the client's outbound segments does detection fall back to the OS TCP retransmission timeout on unacked data — which is finite (Windows ~20-40 s, macOS ~1-2 min, Linux ~15 min worst case), after which the socket errors and `onclose` fires. Browsers on Windows/macOS also tear down sockets on network-interface change/resume. So "no reconnect... ever" is wrong; the worst case is a delayed reconnect on a Linux client behind a black-holing NAT in an explicitly remote-enabled deployment.

3. During any such window, `run.subscribe{fromSeq}` replay (client.ts:66-69) and REST reconciliation still recover missed frames once the reconnect happens, so no data is lost — only delayed.

Net: not a correctness bug in the studio's intended (local) use; at most a latency-of-detection hardening for the opt-in remote mode. The proposed fix is harmless and cheap if the team wants it, but it is not required.

refuted.claim: The search pane re-runs the full workspace search on every fs.changed broadcast, so a running solver that writes result directories repeatedly turns each write into another regex scan of the workspace.
reasons: The scenario as described is largely already handled and partly wrong. (1) "No debounce": the fs.changed events are debounced server-side in /home/user/Iteration-CFD/gui/server/src/workspace/watch.ts (default debounceMs = 300; all chokidar events in a window are collected into `pending` and flushed as ONE broadcast). A solver writing a time directory (U, p, k, epsilon, ... files) therefore produces a single fs.changed broadcast per write, not one per file — the "burst" is coalesced before it reaches the client, so adding a second 300 ms client timer would change essentially nothing. (2) "Flickering results": SearchPane.run() never clears `result` while a re-run is in flight; setResult only happens when the newest request completes (seq guard), so the hit list stays stable — only the small spinner appears. Stale responses are dropped. (3) "Keeping the server busy": the pane is only mounted while the Search activity is selected (SidePanel.tsx renders <SearchPane /> only when activity === 'search'), and re-runs happen at most once per solver write event (writeInterval granularity, seconds apart in both real and mock solvers), each a bounded streamed scan (files > 2 MB skipped, hit cap). The finding also proposes skipping results/time directories, which would be a regression — result dirs (<stem>_jsonc/<time>/...) are deliberately not on the HIDDEN_DIRS list and users legitimately search them. What remains is a minor, by-design cost: one workspace re-scan per fs.changed broadcast while the search pane is open, with no cancellation of an in-flight request if scans outlast the write interval. That is a low-value optimisation, not a correctness or responsiveness defect.

Holds in substance, with two corrections. Reachability: solver output goes to `<stem>_jsonc/` (or the foam case dir) beside the case, i.e. inside the watched workspace (`server/src/main.ts` only ignores runsDir/sessionsDir/cacheDir; `HIDDEN_DIRS` in `server/src/workspace/paths.ts` does not hide result/time dirs), so each solver write (mock: `writer.write` per writeInterval, default endTime/5; real: per writeInterval) produces an `fs.changed`. `SearchPane.tsx:50` subscribes with `fsEvents.subscribe(() => void run())` — no coalescing and no in-flight guard — and `api.search` (`web/src/api/rest.ts`) passes no AbortSignal, so each broadcast starts a fresh `searchWorkspace` that walks the whole workspace (default `workspaceRoot` is the repo root: rust/, docs/, gui/... minus node_modules/target/dist/.git/reference) streaming every text file <=2 MB through readline. If a scan takes longer than the gap between broadcasts, scans run concurrently server-side; the `seq` ref only discards stale responses, it cancels nothing. Correction 1 (severity): the server watcher (`server/src/workspace/watch.ts`) already coalesces events into at most one broadcast per 300 ms, so the "every 100 iterations => burst" is mostly absorbed; only writes lasting >300 ms (large ASCII fields) yield several broadcasts 300 ms apart. And "flickering results" is overstated: stale responses are dropped by `seq`, `collapsed` is keyed by path and persists, identical hits reconcile with no visible change — only the busy spinner blinks. So low severity is right; it is a wasted-work/pile-up issue, not a UX-breaking one. Correction 2 (fix): the proposed "skip when changed paths are inside results/time directories" is wrong — result files are searchable (not hidden) and a query matching them must refresh; drop that part. The debounce + in-flight guard is the right fix.
